To fix Codebook Check

What we found

  • We parsed 57 variable definitions from codebook/README files.
  • 59 of 297 data columns (20%) are documented in a codebook; 238 are not.
  • 3 matched columns have a conflicting or ambiguous label that needs resolution.
Show details

This module checks whether each extracted data column is documented in a codebook or README, and flags documented variables that never appear in the data.

We examined 2 codebook/README/label sources and 297 data columns across 17 files.

To check (4)

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 3 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Text Sentence
p = .961 The control and other-crisis conditions did not differ from each other (p = .961, d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.25]).
p = .691 The difference between the control and other-crisis conditions was not significant (p = .691, d = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.31, 0.13]).
p = .762 These two conditions did not differ from each other (p = .762, d = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.30]).

For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see:

Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742.

Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167.

For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see Improving Your Statistical Inferences.

  • We could not check 3 repositories: https://osf.io/dc38b (private); https://osf.io/bgyzs (private); https://osf.io/v9qyx (private).

  • We found 12 file naming problems to fix.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 19 distinct packages/libraries: boot, car, correlation, dplyr, effectsize, emmeans, ggpubr, ggrepel, ggthemes, haven, knitr, lme4, lmerTest, multcomp, pander, parallel, psych, sjPlot, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

1690 1 R_8CPy17Erzh8EKAp PL 1 2 69 1 4 18 4 12.519 116.400 172.516 8 NA Na jakimś statku wycieczkowym stwierdzono zachorowanie hantawirusem. W Polsce izolowano jedną osobę, która mogła mieć kontakt z zakażonymi. Z tego powodu powstało bardzo silne zagrożenie epidemiologiczne (tak napisali, chociaż mnie to śmieszy, bo już widzę za rok-dwa nagonkę na nowe szczepienie potrzebne tylko do nabijania kasy firmom farmaceutycznym). Drugi wątek to wzrost zachorowań wywołanych bakteriami lekoodpornymi (to też mnie śmieszy, bo bakterie skutecznie uśmierca się antybiotykami, tylko że wcześniej trzeba ustalić, na co ta bakteria jest odporna, a na co nie - sformułowanie “bakteria lekoodporna” jest bzdurą, bo przecież aspiryna jest lekiem, ale bakterii nie tłucze, bo nie jest antybiotykiem; poza tym, różne szczepy różnych bakterii są odporne na niektóre antybiotyki, a na inne nie, zatem przed podaniem antybiotyku lekarz powinien zlecić odpowiednie testy; w konsekwencji - wzrost zachorowań bakteryjnych może wskazywać wyłącznie na niesprawności intelektualne lekarzy i na nic więcej). W konkluzji artykułu znalazło się stwierdzenie, że przypadek hantawirusa w Polsce (zresztą nie potwierdzony) + wzrost zachorowań bakteryjnych stanowi ogromne zagrożenie epidemiologiczne (co jest w mojej opinii czystą “sensacomanią”). This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 297 columns across 17 data files.

Issues Identified

16 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

29 distinct respondents were flagged for straightlining: giving the same answer for at least 80% of the items in a multi-item scale of 5 items or more. One respondent can be flagged in several scales; the table below is one row per person, and the Longest run column gives the run that triggered the strongest flag, so you can check it against the raw data.

Of these, 29 were flagged only by short-scale straightlining (a run of identical answers on a scale of 7 items or fewer). On a short, one-directional scale, answering consistently is often normal, coherent responding rather than carelessness — treat these as weak signals and inspect the actual responses before excluding anyone.

These are prompts to inspect those rows, not definitive judgements.

What this does not cover. Only 1 of 17 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A script runs longer than our limit of 5 minutes.

  • Study2-supplementary analyses-murray.R
  • Study2-supplementary analyses-murray.Rmd
  • Study2-supplementary analyses.R
  • Study2-supplementary analyses.Rmd

State in the README how long each script runs. If some steps take hours, save their results (such as fitted models) to files, add those to the deposit, and let the script read them, so readers can check the rest without waiting.

Comparison with the paper

Of the 37 statistical tests reported in the paper, 19 were found in the output of the code.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 16 R code files.

File paths

2 data paths in the code do not work in the repository as deposited. We pointed them to where the file is, so the code could run: jespfocal.csv to ../jespfocal.csv (in Study 1-supplementary analyses.Rmd); jespfocal.csv to ../jespfocal.csv (in Study-1-supplementary-analyses.R). The code should be changed, because as written it does not find these files.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 16 scripts: 12 ran without error, 0 errored, 4 timed out, 0 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse. Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.

> descriptives <- function(dataset) {
>   results <- tibble(
>     scale = names(scales),
>     Alpha = NA_character_,
>     r     = NA_character_,

>     N     = NA_integer_
>   )
> 
>   for (scale_name in names(scales)) {

>     num_items <- ncol(scale_data)
> 
>     if (num_items == 1) {
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, "-"),
>                r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     } else if (num_items == 2) {
>       corr_value <- round(cor(scale_data[[1]], scale_data[[2]], use = "complete.obs"), 2)
>       results <- results %>%

>     } else if (num_items > 2) {
>       alpha_res   <- alpha(scale_data)
>       alpha_value <- round(alpha_res$total$raw_alpha, 2)

>     }
>

>   }
> 
>   pander(results)
> }

> scales <- list(
>   Generic_consp        = c("Generic_1", "Generic_2", "Generic_3", "Generic_5", "Generic_6"),
>   vaccine              = c("vaccine"),
>   Perceived_prevalence = c("prevalence1", "prevalence2_", "prevalence3_"),
>   Political_orientation = c("polit")
> )
> descriptives <- function(dataset) {
>   results <- tibble(
>     scale = names(scales),
>     Alpha = NA_character_,
>     r     = NA_character_,
>     M     = NA_real_,
>     SD    = NA_real_,
>     N     = NA_integer_
>   )
> 
>   for (scale_name in names(scales)) {
>     scale_data <- dplyr::select(dataset, dplyr::all_of(scales[[scale_name]]))
>     num_items <- ncol(scale_data)
> 
>     if (num_items == 1) {
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, "-"),
>                r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     } else if (num_items == 2) {
>       corr_value <- round(cor(scale_data[[1]], scale_data[[2]], use = "complete.obs"), 2)
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, corr_value),
>                Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     } else if (num_items > 2) {
>       alpha_res   <- alpha(scale_data)
>       alpha_value <- round(alpha_res$total$raw_alpha, 2)
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, alpha_value),
>                r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     }
> 
>     scale_mean   <- round(mean(rowMeans(scale_data, na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
>     scale_sd     <- round(sd(rowMeans(scale_data, na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
>     observations <- nrow(scale_data)
> 
>     results <- results %>%
>       mutate(M = replace(M, scale == scale_name, scale_mean),
>              SD = replace(SD, scale == scale_name, scale_sd),
>              N  = replace(N, scale == scale_name, observations))
>   }
> 
>   pander(results)
> }

> scales <- list(
>   Generic_consp        = c("Generic_1", "Generic_2", "Generic_3", "Generic_5", "Generic_6"),
>   vaccine              = c("vaccine"),
>   Perceived_prevalence = c("prevalence1", "prevalence2_", "prevalence3_"),
>   Political_orientation = c("polit")
> )
> descriptives <- function(dataset) {
>   results <- tibble(
>     scale = names(scales),
>     Alpha = NA_character_,
>     r     = NA_character_,
>     M     = NA_real_,
>     SD    = NA_real_,
>     N     = NA_integer_
>   )
> 
>   for (scale_name in names(scales)) {
>     scale_data <- dplyr::select(dataset, dplyr::all_of(scales[[scale_name]]))
>     num_items <- ncol(scale_data)
> 
>     if (num_items == 1) {
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, "-"),
>                r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     } else if (num_items == 2) {
>       corr_value <- round(cor(scale_data[[1]], scale_data[[2]], use = "complete.obs"), 2)
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, corr_value),
>                Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     } else if (num_items > 2) {
>       alpha_res   <- alpha(scale_data)
>       alpha_value <- round(alpha_res$total$raw_alpha, 2)
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, alpha_value),
>                r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     }
> 
>     scale_mean   <- round(mean(rowMeans(scale_data, na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
>     scale_sd     <- round(sd(rowMeans(scale_data, na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
>     observations <- nrow(scale_data)
> 
>     results <- results %>%
>       mutate(M = replace(M, scale == scale_name, scale_mean),
>              SD = replace(SD, scale == scale_name, scale_sd),
>              N  = replace(N, scale == scale_name, observations))
>   }
> 
>   pander(results)
> }

> scales <- list(
>   Generic_consp        = c("Generic_1", "Generic_2", "Generic_3", "Generic_5", "Generic_6"),
>   vaccine              = c("vaccine"),
>   Perceived_prevalence = c("prevalence1", "prevalence2_", "prevalence3_"),

> )
> descriptives <- function(dataset) {
>   results <- tibble(
>     scale = names(scales),
>     Alpha = NA_character_,
>     r     = NA_character_,
>     M     = NA_real_,
>     SD    = NA_real_,
>     N     = NA_integer_
>   )
> 
>   for (scale_name in names(scales)) {
>     scale_data <- dplyr::select(dataset, dplyr::all_of(scales[[scale_name]]))
>     num_items <- ncol(scale_data)
> 
>     if (num_items == 1) {
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, "-"),
>                r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     } else if (num_items == 2) {
>       corr_value <- round(cor(scale_data[[1]], scale_data[[2]], use = "complete.obs"), 2)
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, corr_value),
>                Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     } else if (num_items > 2) {
>       alpha_res   <- alpha(scale_data)
>       alpha_value <- round(alpha_res$total$raw_alpha, 2)
>       results <- results %>%
>         mutate(Alpha = replace(Alpha, scale == scale_name, alpha_value),
>                r     = replace(r, scale == scale_name, "-"))
>     }
> 
>     scale_mean   <- round(mean(rowMeans(scale_data, na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
>     scale_sd     <- round(sd(rowMeans(scale_data, na.rm = TRUE)), 2)
>     observations <- nrow(scale_data)
> 
>     results <- results %>%
>       mutate(M = replace(M, scale == scale_name, scale_mean),
>              SD = replace(SD, scale == scale_name, scale_sd),
>              N  = replace(N, scale == scale_name, observations))
>   }
> 
>   pander(results)
> }

Reported vs. reproduced

37 statistical tests reported in the manuscript text were checked against the extracted analysis output: 19 matched (9 fully, 10 partially) — 51.4% found.

Some reported values were only found alongside OTHER components after being separated from their own originally-reported neighbours (e.g. a mean split from its own confidence interval). The “Plausible” column marks whether that split is well-supported: TRUE when the pieces still trace back to the same underlying variable (via the output’s own row labels), FALSE when no such link was found — a FALSE match is not necessarily wrong, but is worth checking against its own Source file/Analysis columns before treating it as confirmed.

SPSS data without syntax

An SPSS data file (.sav/.por) is present but no SPSS syntax file (.sps) was found, so the analysis that produced the results cannot be reproduced from the deposit. This is treated as a reproducibility failure (red). Consider depositing the analysis in jamovi (.omv) or JASP (.jasp) instead: these formats store the data and the analyses together in one file, so the results are reproducible from the file itself.

More detail

Ethics Approval Check

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, and it was present:

Dataset 1 (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023) used a validated single-item measure of generic conspiracy beliefs (Lantian et al., 2016), in which participants were presented with a preamble describing how official versions of political and social events may hide the truth.

In some countries, respondents were compensated with course credit or monetary rewards, with values depending on the local context.

Informed consent was obtained from the participants prior to survey completion.

Participants were US residents aged 18 and older.

Participants (Polish adults) were recruited through an external panel provider (Pollster).

After applying the preregistered exclusion criteria, the final sample comprised 493 participants (51.1% women; M age = 48.52, SD age = 16.97), with 166 of them in the pathogen prevalence condition, 169 in the other-crisis condition, and 158 in the control condition.

Next, participants completed a short, openended task in which they summarized the article, followed by the conspiracy belief measures.

After completing the measures, participants were debriefed.

Participants were presented with three items, e.g., “There are currently many infectious diseases around me,” and were asked to rate each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

The analyses of the remaining 490 participants were virtually identical to the previously reported results and all conclusions remained unchanged.

Ethics approval statement:

Research Ethics Committees of [masked for review] provided ethics approvals for Study 2.

The Research Ethics Committee of the [masked for review] provided the ethics approval for Study 4.

Power Analysis Check

We used the LLM model ‘vllm/qwen3-8-27b-fp8’ to check the contents of 2 paragraphs that contained words suggesting they might contain power analyses.

All essential information could be detected.

power_type statistical_test sample_size alpha_level power effect_size effect_size_metric software
apriori 1-way ANOVA 495 0.05 0.8 0.14 Cohen’s f G*Power
text
We determined the target sample size with an a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007). According to Biddlestone et al. (2025) in their meta-analysis of motives associated with conspiracy beliefs, correlations between these motives and conspiracy beliefs range from r = .14 to r = .16. We took the lower bound as the expected effect size and converted it to Cohen’s f, yielding f = .14. A one-way fixed-effects ANOVA with three groups, α = .05, and power = .80 required 495 participants. We set a recruitment target of 550 participants to retain adequate power after exclusions. Following preregistration, we excluded participants who failed an attention check included in the conspiracy belief items, provided an invalid response to the post-article recall task (answering incorrectly, nonsensically, or offtopic), or left any scale incomplete.

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

Conspiracy beliefs data: The data come from the 50-state, nonprobability, web-based survey conducted by the COVID States Project via Pure Spectrum. The survey used state-by-state quotas for age, gender, and race/ethnicity. Participants were US residents aged 18 and older (N = 123,781).

Pathogen prevalence data: State-level infectious disease prevalence scores come from Fincher and Thornhill (2012). This measure aggregates all infectious diseases reported by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) for each state from 1993 to 2007, divides by state population, and transforms the result into a z-score. 		The target population is adults living in Poland. Participants will be recruited online through a panel administered by an external company and will complete the study on Qualtrics. To be eligible, participants must be at least 18 years old and must complete the study on a desktop computer or laptop, as the survey is not available on mobile devices. After consent and demographic questions, Qualtrics will randomly assign each participant to one of the three conditions (pathogen prevalence, other-crisis, control) in approximately equal proportions. sample_size_rationale At the country level, we aim to include as many countries as possible for power and generalizability. As a heuristic, to achieve .80 power (α = .05) to detect a medium country-level association (r ≈ .40), at least 44 country observations are required; therefore, the minimum target was set at 50 countries, with the goal to exceed this if possible. At the individual level, the minimum target within each country is 200. NA We anchored the expected effect size to the meta-analysis by Biddlestone et al. (2025), which examined motivations for conspiracy beliefs and reported correlation coefficients ranging from r = 0.14 to r = 0.16. Converting the lower bound (r = 0.14) to Cohen’s f yields an expected effect of approximately f = 0.14 for our main manipulation. A power analysis using G*Power indicated that detecting an effect of f = 0.14 with alpha = 0.05 and power = 0.80 requires 495 participants. We plan to recruit 550 participants to account for potential exclusions due to missing data or failed attention checks.

statistical_tests We will test a 2-1-1 multilevel mediation model with individuals nested within countries (with random intercepts and random slopes). Bivariate Pearson correlation between state-level infectious disease prevalence (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012) and state-level means of all four ACTS conspiracy items (Perlis et al., 2025). Manipulation check: A one-way ANOVA on perceived pathogen prevalence with experimental condition as the between-subjects factor, followed by Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons. We expect the pathogen prevalence condition to score higher than the control and other-crisis conditions.

H1 and H2: A one-way ANOVA on each measure of conspiracy beliefs with experimental condition as the between-subjects factor, followed by Tukey HSD post-hoc comparisons. H1 is tested by the pathogen prevalence vs. control comparison, and H2 by the pathogen prevalence vs. other-crisis comparison.

The latter check verifies that any effect of the pathogen prevalence manipulation is not driven by participants spontaneously thinking about the COVID-19 pandemic rather than the infectious-disease prevalence described in the article.
