Study 4 Method

Aims and hypotheses

Studies 1-3 provided evidence for a positive relationship between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs across countries and US states. However, because these designs were correlational, they cannot establish the direction of the relationship. Study 4 employed an experimental design to test whether heightened perceived pathogen prevalence increases conspiracy beliefs. Participants read one of three newspaper-style articles. The pathogen prevalence article described a novel hantavirus outbreak; the other-crisis article described a societal crisis unrelated to infectious disease (housing crisis); and the control condition article described a neutral topic (urban transportation). Hantavirus received media attention in spring 2026, when an outbreak on a cruise ship was attributed to human-tohuman transmission (see e.g., Roberts, 2026).

We expected participants in the heightened pathogen prevalence condition to report stronger conspiracy beliefs than those in the control condition (H1). The other-crisis condition allowed us to examine whether the effect of the manipulation is specific to disease salience or if it is a response to information about any kind of crisis. Therefore, we also expected conspiracy beliefs to be stronger in the heightened pathogen prevalence condition than in the other-crisis condition (H2). The hypotheses, design, and analytic approach were preregistered on the Open Science Framework (https://osf.io/v9qyx/overview?view_only=ec3b61033c1a4e8b923fadab71ddbcb3).

Participants

Participants (Polish adults) were recruited through an external panel provider (Pollster). To avoid issues with visibility of the articles they had to complete the study on a computer. We collected data from 533 participants. After applying the preregistered exclusion criteria, the final sample comprised 493 participants (51.1% women; M age = 48.52, SD age = 16.97), with 166 of them in the pathogen prevalence condition, 169 in the other-crisis condition, and 158 in the control condition.

We determined the target sample size with an a priori power analysis in G*Power (Faul et al., 2007). According to Biddlestone et al. (2025) in their meta-analysis of motives associated with conspiracy beliefs, correlations between these motives and conspiracy beliefs range from r = .14 to r = .16. We took the lower bound as the expected effect size and converted it to Cohen's f, yielding f = .14. A one-way fixed-effects ANOVA with three groups, α = .05, and power = .80 required 495 participants. We set a recruitment target of 550 participants to retain adequate power after exclusions. Following preregistration, we excluded participants who failed an attention check included in the conspiracy belief items, provided an invalid response to the post-article recall task (answering incorrectly, nonsensically, or offtopic), or left any scale incomplete.

Procedure

The study was administered online through Qualtrics. After providing informed consent, participants reported their demographics. Then, they were randomly assigned to one of three conditions and read the corresponding article. To encourage careful reading, the option to continue was disabled for three minutes. Next, participants completed a short, openended task in which they summarized the article, followed by the conspiracy belief measures. Next, they described what they had been thinking about while reading and completed the perceived pathogen prevalence items. Finally, they were asked whether they had heard of Hantavirus before taking part in the study.

All three articles that served as the manipulation stimuli were written for this study and formatted to resemble reports from an online news service. The articles were matched in terms of length and structure, and each included quotations attributed to experts. The article in the pathogen prevalence condition described an outbreak of a novel, human-transmissible hantavirus, as well as rising antibiotic resistance. The article in the other-crisis condition described a housing market crisis and related infrastructure failures. The control condition article described urban transportation and cycling. The full texts of the three articles with translations are provided in the Supplementary Materials (Figures S6-S8). After completing the measures, participants were debriefed. The debriefing explained that the articles had been prepared for research purposes only and did not describe a current public health threat, and directed participants to official public health sources.

Measures

Generic conspiracist beliefs (ɑ = .84) were measured using the five-item Generic Conspiracist Beliefs Scale (Kay & Slovic, 2023), which is a shortened version of Brotherton et al.'s (2013) 15-item scale. Participants rated their agreement with each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 6 (strongly agree).

Vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs were measured with a single item (Toribio-Florez et al., 2025): "Scientists work together to cover up the dangers of vaccines" which was rated on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree).

Perceived pathogen prevalence (ɑ = .83) was measured as a manipulation check. Participants were presented with three items, e.g., "There are currently many infectious diseases around me," and were asked to rate each item on a scale ranging from 1 (strongly disagree) to 7 (strongly agree). The full list of items is presented in the Supplementary Materials.

Analytic strategy

We analyzed the data using one-way ANOVAs with Tukey HSD comparisons. First, we tested the effectiveness of the manipulation by comparing perceived pathogen prevalence across the three conditions. Then, we tested our hypotheses about generic conspiracist beliefs by comparing the pathogen prevalence condition with the control condition (H1) and the other-crisis condition (H2). The vaccine conspiracy belief item was analyzed in the same way. We preregistered two robustness checks. Since prior familiarity with the disease could weaken the manipulation, we planned to repeat the analyses after excluding participants who reported having heard of the Hantavirus before the study. Additionally, because thinking of experience during the COVID-19 pandemic could influence responses to an article about infectious diseases, we planned to code open-ended responses for spontaneous mentions of the COVID-19 pandemic and to repeat the analyses after excluding participants who mentioned it. The results of these analyses are presented in the Supplementary Materials.

Results

Manipulation check

A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of condition on perceived pathogen prevalence, F(2, 490) = 5.39, p = .005, η² = .02. Tukey HSD comparisons showed that participants in the pathogen prevalence condition perceived a higher prevalence of pathogens (M = 3.34, SE = 0.10) than those in the control condition (M = 2.95, SE = 0.11; p = .021, d = 0.30, 95% CI [0.08, 0.52]) and the other-crisis condition (M = 2.91, SE = 0.10; p = .008, d = 0.33, 95% CI [0.11, 0.54]). The control and other-crisis conditions did not differ from each other (p = .961, d = 0.03, 95% CI [-0.19, 0.25]).

Generic conspiracist beliefs

A one-way ANOVA revealed a significant effect of condition, F(2, 490) = 8.28, p < .001, η² = .03. Consistent with H1, participants in the pathogen prevalence condition reported higher levels of generic conspiracist beliefs (M = 3.09, SE = 0.09) than those in the control condition (M = 2.58, SE = 0.09; p < .001, d = 0.43, 95% CI [0.21, 0.65]). Also, in line with H2, they reported higher levels of generic conspiracist beliefs than participants in the othercrisis condition (M = 2.69, SE = 0.09; p = .006, d = 0.34, 95% CI [0.12, 0.55]). The difference between the control and other-crisis conditions was not significant (p = .691, d = -0.09, 95% CI [-0.31, 0.13]).

Vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs

The same pattern emerged in the case of the vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs, for which we also found a significant main effect of condition, F(2, 490) = 9.82, p < .001, η² = .04. Vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs were highest in the pathogen prevalence condition (M = 4.09, SE = 0.14), compared to both the control condition (M = 3.39, SE = 0.15; p = .002, d = 0.38, 95% CI [0.16, 0.60]) and the other-crisis condition (M = 3.25, SE = 0.14; p < .001, d = 0.45, 95% CI [0.24, 0.67]). These two conditions did not differ from each other (p = .762, d = 0.08, 95% CI [-0.14, 0.30]).

Additional analyses

Two preregistered robustness checks (Tables S11 and S12 in the Supplementary Materials) were conducted. In the first analysis, participants who spontaneously mentioned the COVID-19 pandemic in the open-ended item were excluded. Only three of the 493 responses contained such mentions. The analyses of the remaining 490 participants were virtually identical to the previously reported results and all conclusions remained unchanged. The second analysis excluded participants who reported having heard of Hantavirus before the study. Of the 493 participants, 305 (61.9%) reported prior familiarity, leaving 188 for this analysis. Retention did not differ significantly across conditions. Within this subsample, the manipulation remained effective. Participants in the pathogen prevalence condition perceived a higher prevalence of pathogens than those in the control and other-crisis conditions. However, the effects of the condition on generic conspiracist beliefs and vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs were not significant. Because only 38.1% of the sample was retained, these analyses had limited power to detect effects of the size observed in the full sample.

General discussion

This research examined the relationship between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs. Study 1 found higher endorsement of various conspiracy beliefs in countries with higher historical pathogen prevalence. Both Study 2, which included a larger cross-national sample, and Study 3, which examined US states, replicated the findings of Study 1. Finally, Study 4 found that manipulating perceived pathogen prevalence increased generic and vaccine-related conspiracy beliefs compared to a neutral article and one about an unrelated societal crisis.

These findings add disease ecology to the societal characteristics associated with conspiracy beliefs, alongside greater corruption (Alper, 2023), weaker economic performance (Hornsey, Pearson, et al., 2023), lower societal freedom (Siemiątkowski et al., 2026), and wartime losses (Bilewicz et al., 2024). Importantly, pathogen prevalence was examined in three forms, differing in timescale and aggregation level. The country-level indices summarize disease burden accumulated across generations, describing the ecological context in which a population developed (Fincher et al., 2008; Murray & Schaller, 2010). The US state-level index reflects incidence recorded by public health surveillance in recent decades (Fincher & Thornhill, 2012). The experimental manipulation concerned how prevalent the disease appeared when measured. These operationalizations are not identical, and their convergence does not prove a single underlying process, but it does suggest that the association is not confined to one index, timescale, or level of measurement. The behavioral immune system framework explains why pathogen prevalence consistently matters across these levels. Evolved pathogen-avoidance mechanisms shape intergroup attitudes by promoting wariness toward unfamiliar others where disease risk is high (Murray & Schaller, 2016; Schaller & Park, 2011). Our findings suggest that this legacy may extend to conspiratorial thinking, possibly because environments of persistent infectious disease foster stronger in-group boundaries and suspicion of outsiders and, given that disease carriers cannot be identified by sight, of hidden agents within one's own society. This aligns with van Prooijen's (2020) existential threat model, in which conspiracy beliefs emerge when existential threats trigger sense-making in the presence of antagonistic outgroups, because pathogen prevalence is a historically persistent ecological stressor that simultaneously heightens existential uncertainty and outgroup vigilance. The experimental results also suggest the effect is specific to disease threat. Were the effect a general reaction to unsettling news, the housing-crisis article should also have raised conspiracy beliefs. Yet that condition was indistinguishable from the neutral-article control on both outcome measures, consistent with accounts in which pathogen cues engage a distinct threat-management system (Neuberg et al., 2011). Similar specificity emerged experimentally for intergroup outcomes, with disease salience reducing positive attitudes toward foreign immigrant groups relative to a salient non-disease threat (Faulkner et al., 2004).

Taken together, the four studies converge on the same association across levels of analysis, measures, and designs. Because the responsible processes remain unidentified and only the experimental design allows a causal interpretation, this research remains an initial examination, constrained by the limitations outlined below. Nevertheless, it points toward a line of inquiry treating conspiracy beliefs as shaped not only by immediate political and informational circumstances but also by ecological conditions persisting over time. If salient disease cues increase conspiratorial thinking, outbreaks could generate not only a public health crisis but also conditions favoring conspiracy theories, undermining the response to the outbreak itself (Bierwiaczonek et al., 2022).

Limitations and future directions

Despite its strengths, our research has several limitations. The macro-level studies were correlational, which limits causal claims. The experiment addressed the direction of the effect, but did so for perceived rather than historical prevalence, and therefore cannot establish that the process it demonstrates generates the cross-national pattern. A related caution concerns the non-pathogen crisis comparison. A single null result indicates that this particular stimulus did not raise conspiracy beliefs, not that non-disease crises are generally ineffective, and testing further crisis types would strengthen the case for specificity.

Additionally, the experimental effects were small to moderate, as expected given that a brief news article is a minimal intervention compared to a lifetime in a disease ecology. Stronger or repeated manipulations and longitudinal designs tracking conspiracy beliefs as disease salience shifts would determine whether these effects grow and persist under sustained exposure. Our designs also do not identify the processes through which disease ecology becomes associated with conspiracy beliefs, whether through culturally transmitted norms of in-group cohesion and wariness toward outsiders, through vigilance activated by contemporary disease cues, or through feelings of anxiety. Furthermore, analyses in Studies 1 and 3 used aggregated scores unadjusted for subsample size in each macro-level unit, a limitation Study 2 addresses with a multilevel model. Moreover, younger respondents and women were overrepresented in the samples of Studies 1 and 2. Finally, the available datasets left certain regions underrepresented, most notably Sub-Saharan Africa, where pathogen prevalence has been historically high. Expanding cross-national research to more countries would allow a more comprehensive evaluation of this framework. Nonetheless, this research is among the largest cross-national examinations of conspiracy beliefs to date.

Conclusion

The present research demonstrated a positive association between pathogen prevalence and conspiracy beliefs across multiple datasets and showed that heightened perceived prevalence increases their endorsement. These findings provide initial evidence that pathogen-rich ecologies may contribute to contemporary conspiracy thinking. Two constraints qualify this conclusion. The macro-level evidence is correlational, so the causal claim rests on a single experiment manipulating perceived rather than historical prevalence, and the included countries and regions underrepresent those with the heaviest historical disease burden. Nevertheless, the convergence of centuries-long ecological indices and a momentary experimental cue suggest that infectious disease prevalence shaped not only how societies organize but what their members are prepared to believe.
